claims.text: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by a balance between thermodynamic driving force for Al-induced chemical ordering and kinetic limitations on atomic diffusion.
This thermodynamic–kinetic balance determines whether the high-temperature BCC phase is retained or transforms by nucleating ordered Al-rich precipitates.
The ordered precipitates may be B2-type.
Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 has a high-temperature single-phase BCC state.
Rapid quenching can preserve the high-temperature BCC state of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Annealing Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 at 600–750 °C activates sufficient atomic diffusion to promote ordering.
The structural mediator is nucleation and growth of nanoscale ordered domains or Al-rich clusters.
At high temperature, the BCC state is metastable because kinetic barriers suppress chemical ordering.
Lower-temperature thermal exposure permits Al and possibly other elements to segregate and form ordered clusters.
Slower cooling or prolonged annealing increases the probability that the BCC phase develops a mixed microstructure containing ordered precipitates.
Annealed samples should contain a larger volume fraction of ordered precipitates than rapidly quenched samples.
Annealed samples should show more local chemical ordering than rapidly quenched samples.
Ordered precipitates or chemical ordering will occur at grain boundaries or within the BCC matrix.
Annealing-induced ordering will produce measurable changes in hardness or ductility.
The rapidly quenched baseline retains a homogeneous BCC structure with minimal chemical ordering.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to conditions in which the alloy is initially single phase and may not apply when impurities or extreme nonequilibrium processing cause extrinsic phase formation.
Failure of annealing to increase ordered precipitates or local Al-associated ordering relative to the quenched control would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Failure of ordering to correlate with thermal treatment would falsify the proposed thermodynamic–kinetic control mechanism.

contradictions.description: The high-temperature regime is called the BCC stability region in the conditions, while the mechanism describes the BCC phase at high temperature as metastable.
